newsitem.title: MEXICO: Fall in Mexico's Cetes rates tempered by inflation.
newsitem.headline: Fall in Mexico's Cetes rates tempered by inflation.

text.p: Mexico's primary Cetes rates fell across the yield curve at the primary auction on Tuesday, but the declines were tempered by concerns over inflation in September and rate volatility in the United States, market analysts said.
"The shorter-term Cetes were probably impacted by things like the September CPI, which will be a little bit higher due to seasonal factors," said MMS International economist Sonia Stromeyer.
The eight-basis point decline in the bellwether 28-day paper brought that rate down to 23.38 percent.
The 91-day paper rate fell 43 basis points to 27.30 percent, while the 182-day Cetes fell 123 basis points to 28.68 percent.
The one-year paper was assigned at 29.18 percent, compared with 30.93 percent the week before, Banco de Mexico said.
"Investors were worried about the future of interest rates in the United States and as of yet have not discounted (Mexico's) September inflation," added another market analyst.
A survey by Reuters of 11 brokerages in Mexico City found forecasts of an average 0.97 percent increase in consumer prices in the first half of September.
Foreign interest in the Cetes has been strong recently, driving up demand.
But this week the bid-to-cover ratio for the auction as a whole was only 3.32 on demand of 10.95 billion pesos compared with 4.58 the week before, on demand of 11.52 billion pesos.
Stromeyer said that the bid-to-cover ratio was unusually low this week, and below the 12-week average.

Demand was stronger for the longer-terms Cetes, and some market analysts said that some clients were looking for longer-term paper to tie up rates with the expectation of lower Mexican inflation next year.
Markets were also nervous on Tuesday due to a report on Reuters that eight of the 12 district banks in the Federal Reserve System have requested a rise in the U.S. discount rate.
The comments knocked at the U.S. Treasury market, causing the yield on the influential 30-year bond to rise to 7.03 percent.
Increases in U.S. interest rates more often than not ripple through Mexican markets.
